args.title: stipulation-markup-analysis.docx
args.body:
MEMORANDUM

TO: Engagement File
FROM: Tax Practice Group
RE: Prioritized Issues Memo — Analysis of IRS Counterparty Markup of Proposed Stipulation of Facts in Carried Interest Tax Court Dispute
DATE: [Current Date]

PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This memorandum analyzes the Internal Revenue Service's counterparty markup of our proposed stipulation of facts in the carried interest Tax Court dispute. We have reconciled the IRS markup against (i) the base deal materials, (ii) the disclosure schedules and exhibits that qualify those materials, and (iii) the latest partnership instruction on analysis priorities. This memo identifies every deviation introduced by the IRS markup, assigns priority based on the controlling client direction, and provides recommendations for each issue.

CONTROLLING PRIORITY FRAMEWORK

Per the latest partner email on this engagement (which supersedes all prior messages in the thread), the client's positions are as follows:

1. The client WILL CONCEDE the basket conversion proposed by the IRS (from a deductible basket to a tipping basket). This issue is therefore not a fighting point and should not be the subject of extended negotiation.
2. ANY reduction to the survival period for the core representations is a WALK-AWAY ISSUE. The IRS's proposed limitation-period shortening is non-negotiable from the client's perspective and, if not resolved, would be grounds for terminating the stipulation negotiation.

Issues are prioritized below on this basis, with highest-risk items addressed first.

ISSUE NO. 1 — CRITICAL / WALK-AWAY: IRS SHORTENS SURVIVAL PERIOD FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS

Deviation Identified: The IRS markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival of the core representations beyond what is provided in the base stipulation.

Base Position: The base stipulation and Exhibit B (the survival matrix) establish a survival framework for the core representations consistent with the firm's standard tax practice and applicable Tax Court rules. The survival periods reflected in Exhibit B are the operative baseline against which all amendments in the markup must be measured. The scheduled exceptions to Exhibit B do not modify the survival period for the core representations, and the base materials treat survival as a defined, fixed term.

IRS Markup: The IRS's revision shortens the survival period applicable to the core representations, deviating from the Exhibit B survival matrix. The scheduled exceptions confirm that the survival framework was deliberately calibrated—with disclosure references and specific carve-outs—and was not intended to be a placeholder subject to silent reduction.

Analysis: A reduction in the survival period is material because it would expose the client to the IRS asserting that certain factual representations cease to be effective prior to the conclusion of the relevant examination or litigation window, prejudicing the client's ability to rely on those stipulations. The schedules confirm that both parties' disclosures contemplate a defined survival period and that the shortening has no evidentiary or scheduling justification. Under the latest partner instruction, any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue: the client will not proceed on terms that shorten survival.

Recommendation: REJECT the IRS's limitation-period reduction in its entirety. Reassert the Exhibit B survival matrix as the operative schedule. If the IRS persists in pressing the shortened period, treat this as grounds for walking away from the stipulation negotiation. Prepare a counter-proposal that reinstates the Exhibit B survival timeline and affirms that the core representations survive for the full stipulated period. Do not deviate from this position.

ISSUE NO. 2 — HIGH PRIORITY: INDemnification CAP SILENTLY REDUCED

Deviation Identified: The IRS markup silently reduces the indemnification cap relative to the base stipulation.

Base Position: The base stipulation contains an indemnification provision with a defined cap. The cap amount in the base materials is the benchmark against which the markup must be measured. Schedule 5.2 identifies a set of retained liabilities that intersect the indemnification framework; any change to the cap would indirectly shift the economic allocation of these retained liabilities.

IRS Markup: The IRS's revision reduces the indemnification cap without notification or explanation—a "silent" change. The cap reduction is consequential because Schedule 5.2 expressly lists retained liabilities that remain with the IRS/respondent side, and reducing the cap would transfer exposure for those liabilities to the client.

Analysis: Unlike the survival issue, the cap reduction is not expressly identified as a walk-away trigger by the latest partner instruction. However, it is a material economic change that shifts risk allocation. Schedule 5.2's retained liabilities would be partially or fully unprotected under the reduced cap, meaning the client would bear costs the base stipulation assigned to the government. The silent nature of the reduction compounds the concern: it was not flagged for negotiation but buried in the markup.

Recommendation: REJECT the silent reduction of the indemnification cap. Restore the cap to the base stipulation amount. Independently of the cap amount, require the IRS to confirm whether the retained liabilities listed in Schedule 5.2 remain within the indemnification coverage. If the IRS maintains the reduced cap, engage in a targeted negotiation on the cap amount only if the survival issue is first resolved favorably, given that the survival period is the controlling walk-away matter. Do not allow the cap reduction to be conceded without a full assessment of Schedule 5.2 liability shifting.

ISSUE NO. 3 — MEDIUM PRIORITY: MAE CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION OF THE TYPE AT ISSUE

Deviation Identified: The IRS markup adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect (MAE) for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this carried interest dispute.

Base Position: The base stipulation's MAE definition does not include carve-outs for regulatory actions. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that are directly relevant to the subject matter of this dispute—namely, inquiries concerning carried interest treatment and related matters. The base definition of MAE applies uniformly without regard to whether the triggering event arises from regulatory action.

IRS Markup: The IRS adds carve-outs to the MAE definition that exclude regulatory action from constituting an MAE. Critically, the type of regulatory action carved out is precisely the kind at issue in this matter. Schedule 3.7's two pending regulatory inquiries squarely intersect these carve-outs.

Analysis: The MAE carve-outs are concerning for two reasons. First, they are substantively overbroad: by declaring that regulatory action of this kind does not constitute an MAE, the IRS is effectively pre-committing to a position that would bar the client from relying on MAE protection for exactly the regulatory exposure disclosed in Schedule 3.7. Second, they are procedurally troubling: the markup appears designed to leverage the carrier's own Schedule 3.7 disclosures against it, using the disclosed regulatory inquiries as the justification for the carve-out while eliminating the very protection those disclosures should provide.

Recommendation: REJECT the MAE carve-outs as drafted. The carve-outs should be narrowed so that they do not sweep in the two regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7. If the IRS insists on some form of regulatory-action carve-out, counter with language that explicitly excludes the two Schedule 3.7 inquiries from any such carve-out, ensuring the MAE definition retains coverage for those specific exposures. This issue is of medium priority relative to the survival and indemnification issues, but it materially undermines the client's position if allowed to stand.

ISSUE NO. 4 — LOW PRIORITY / CONCEDED: BASKET CONVERTED FROM DEDUCTIBLE TO TIPPING

Deviation Identified: The IRS markup converts the indemnification basket from a deductible basket to a tipping basket.

Base Position: The base stipulation provides for a deductible basket mechanism, under which losses must exceed the basket threshold before any indemnification is payable, with the client bearing losses up to the threshold.

IRS Markup: The IRS converts the basket to a tipping basket, under which once the threshold is exceeded, the indemnifying party is responsible for all losses from the first dollar (including the amount below the threshold).

Analysis: Under the controlling partner instruction, the client HAS CONCEDED the basket conversion. This means the client accepts that the indemnification basket will operate as a tipping basket rather than a deductible basket. The concession should be documented and the final stipulation updated accordingly. Because the client has conceded this point, no further negotiation is warranted on the basket mechanism itself.

Recommendation: CONCEDE (per controlling partner instruction). Update the stipulation to reflect the tipping basket mechanism. Ensure the concession is not coupled with the cap reduction (Issue No. 2), which remains subject to challenge. The basket concession is independent of the cap amount and should not be used as leverage by the IRS to press the cap reduction.

ISSUE NO. 5 — RECONCILIATION OF SCHEDULED EXCEPTIONS AGAINST MARKUP

Deviation Identified: The disclosure schedules (3.7 and 5.2) and Exhibit B form part of the operative base materials. Each scheduled exception interacts with one or more of the markup deviations described above.

Analysis: The scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. This means that in analyzing any deviation, the operative baseline is the schedule-qualified version of the stipulation:

- Schedule 3.7's two pending regulatory inquiries must be read into the MAE analysis (Issue No. 3). The carve-outs are especially harmful because the schedule already puts the client on notice of these inquiries, and the IRS's carve-outs would strip the client of any recourse when those inquiries mature into adverse action.

- Schedule 5.2's retained liabilities are directly impacted by the cap reduction (Issue No. 2). The schedules identify specific liabilities that the IRS's markup would silently shift to the client.

- Exhibit B's survival matrix is the operative baseline for the survival period (Issue No. 1). The IRS's limitation-period change directly conflicts with Exhibit B.

Recommendation: Any final stipulation must expressly incorporate the schedules and exhibit by reference and confirm that the scheduled exceptions control. The IRS markup's deviations must each be evaluated against the schedule-qualified baseline, not against the unqualified general text.

PRIORITIZATION SUMMARY

| Priority | Issue | Client Position | Recommended Action |
|----------|-------|-----------------|-------------------|
| 1 (Critical / Walk-Away) | Survival-period reduction for core representations (Issue No. 1) | Walk-away if not resolved | Reject in full; restore Exhibit B survival matrix; walk away if IRS persists |
| 2 (High) | Silent indemnification cap reduction (Issue No. 2) | Defend unless survival resolved favorably | Reject; restore base cap; assess Schedule 5.2 shift before any concession |
| 3 (Medium) | MAE carve-outs for regulatory action (Issue No. 3) | Defend coverage for Schedule 3.7 inquiries | Reject as drafted; counter with carve-out excluding Schedule 3.7 inquiries |
| 4 (Low / Conceded) | Basket converted from deductible to tipping (Issue No. 4) | Conceded | Accept; document concession; decouple from cap reduction |

CONCLUSION

The IRS markup introduces four material deviations from the proposed stipulation of facts. Three require affirmative resistance, and one has been conceded by the client. The survival-period reduction is the controlling walk-away issue and must be resolved first and favorably. The cap reduction is the second priority and should not be conceded without full assessment of Schedule 5.2 liability shifting. The MAE carve-outs are protectable through narrower counter-language. The basket conversion is conceded and should be memorialized.

The misfiled administrative correspondence (from an unrelated engagement) has been identified and excluded from this analysis. It bears no relevance to the stipulation issues addressed herein.

Prepared by the Tax Practice Group for the engagement file.
